Introduce this as a software simulation of coordination in agricultural IoT. The central contribution is selecting temporary role holders using recursive capability, migration costs, and lease rules. The supplied folder does not identify the student, institution, department, or guide, so replace the marked fields before presenting. The implementation and stored experiments support statements about this model, not a deployed farm network. Allow about 18 minutes for slides 1–33 and use the appendix for questions.

Implementation evidence: Project.md; simulation/config.py

Panel prompt: Explain the implementation boundary and the tradeoff shown on this slide.
Project overview
Python simulation of a fixed logical hierarchy over a physical multi-hop mesh
100 nodes, 10 subnets, 3 networks, 1 internetwork by default
Four role labels at 14 scopes produce 56 required assignments
Users: researchers and students comparing coordination policies
simulation/config.py; simulation/entities.py; nodes.py

Explain the distinction between a role and a scope. A gateway role exists separately for each subnet, each network, and the internetwork. Candidates are immediate children: nodes within a subnet, subnets within a network, and networks at the root. The system measures service availability and communication costs under changing conditions. Anomaly detection, health monitoring, and discoverability are role labels and scores. The code does not implement their application payload services. Transition to why reassignment is useful.

Implementation evidence: simulation/config.py; simulation/entities.py; nodes.py

Panel prompt: Explain the implementation boundary and the tradeoff shown on this slide.
Problem statement
Fixed role holders may remain assigned after their energy or connectivity deteriorates
Global coordination creates a dependency on a controller in the modeled baselines
Frequent reassignment consumes communication energy and can cause instability
The engineering problem is balancing capability improvement against switching cost
Project.md; simulation/protocols.py; simulation/runner.py

Present this as the problem investigated by the project rather than a claim about every IoT deployment. Node energy and link quality affect both suitability and communication. Choosing the highest current score at every step can produce unnecessary churn. Keeping every original holder can leave roles unavailable. The simulator creates a controlled way to compare those policies on the same initial world and event schedule. Ask the panel to judge the mechanism and the evidence under the stated abstraction.

Implementation evidence: Project.md; simulation/protocols.py; simulation/runner.py

Motivation and objectives
Preserve useful role availability when nodes fail or conditions change
Reuse the same role semantics across hierarchy levels
Account for routed control traffic, data traffic, and endpoint energy
Make experiments repeatable with seeded inputs and replayable events
Project.md; FINAL_SPRINT_PLAN.md; simulation/events.py

The specification motivates agricultural networks with distributed, potentially solar-powered devices. In implementation, this becomes a deterministic experiment framework. Its objectives are observable: capability refresh, temporary assignments, failure recovery, and separate communication counters. Solar harvesting is a later implemented extension. Do not suggest that the project contains real agricultural sensor readings or hardware measurements. The hierarchy is an input assumption, so automatic clustering is outside the current objectives.

Panel prompt: Explain the implementation boundary and the tradeoff shown on this slide.
Implemented comparison policies
simulation/protocols.py; simulation/runner.py

Read each row as the exact policy in this codebase. The hierarchical baseline chooses a seeded random fixed controller and random reachable eligible holders, retaining them until failure. Centralized instead uses a fixed controller selected by normalized degree and capability-based reassignment. Static stops policy updates after initialization. Dynamic has local control sources and immediately selects the best reachable score. Proposed adds cost-aware optional migration and leases. These are custom model baselines, not implementations of LEACH, RPL, or another named networking standard.

Implementation evidence: simulation/protocols.py; simulation/runner.py

Panel prompt: Explain the implementation boundary and the tradeoff shown on this slide.
Proposed solution
Compute a role capability vector for each online node
Aggregate child vectors bottom-up through the logical hierarchy
Grant one temporary lease for each role and scope
Migrate only when the candidate clears utility and hysteresis checks
Route control exchanges and sensor load through the physical mesh
simulation/capability.py; simulation/protocols.py; simulation/communications.py

Describe the mechanism as several cooperating modules. The capability calculation says who is suitable. The protocol engine decides whether a change is justified. The lease state machine records who currently holds a role. The router makes communication success and energy visible. The system is decentralized in modeled control-source selection, but one Mesa model executes the simulation in a single process. It does not implement distributed consensus or independent devices exchanging real packets.

Implementation evidence: simulation/capability.py; simulation/protocols.py; simulation/communications.py

Panel prompt: Explain the implementation boundary and the tradeoff shown on this slide.
Technology stack and tradeoffs
requirements.txt; nodes.py; simulation/*.py; patent-study/analyze_patent_study.py

These responsibilities are visible in imports and code. Mesa supplies agent identity and a model clock, while transitions enforces legal state changes. NumPy supplies seeded random generators and numeric operations. Pandas exports and aggregates metrics. Matplotlib produces plots. SciPy is used for t intervals by the study analyzer, but requirements.txt does not declare it. The original specification mentions SimPy and NetworkX, but the active simulator uses neither. Adjacency dictionaries and a custom heap-based router implement the graph behavior. These rationales are architectural interpretations, not recorded author interviews. Environment verification found that Mesa 3.5.1 conflicts with assigning a string to model.scenario. Short simulations work with Mesa 3.3.1. Pin and test a compatible Mesa version before the live demo. NetworkX is a Mesa dependency in this environment, but this project does not use it directly for topology or routing.

Physical mesh and logical hierarchy
LOGICAL CANDIDATES
Internetwork: 1
Networks: 3
Subnets: 10
Physical nodes: 100
PHYSICAL COMMUNICATION
Position-based undirected edges
Optional intercluster bridges
Quality-weighted shortest paths
First online descendant represents a container
simulation/topology.py; simulation/entities.py

Read the left chain as candidate membership, not radio links. The default subnet distribution is 4, 3, and 3. A container is available if at least one descendant node is online. Its representative is the first available descendant in stored order, not necessarily its best gateway. On the physical side, distance creates undirected edges and normalized degree supplies centrality. Positive intercluster spacing also inserts nearest bridge links between adjacent clusters. These long-range links are an abstraction and can exceed the nominal communication range. No hierarchy relationship automatically provides a route.

Implementation evidence: simulation/topology.py; simulation/entities.py

Panel prompt: Explain the implementation boundary and the tradeoff shown on this slide.
Simulation tick workflow

Apply events +
depletion

Refresh scores +
policy decisions

Harvest +
route traffic

Depletion +
metrics
Capabilities refresh again after communication energy changes.
All protocol variants use this same coordinator and event schedule.
simulation/runner.py: RoleSimulationModel.step

Mesa advances the step count and invokes the model step. Apply scheduled events first and fail depleted nodes. Refresh capabilities before policy decisions so failure and degradation influence selection. Mark affected scopes if configured, then update leases and migrations. Harvest solar energy after protocol decisions and before sensor traffic. Route sensor and optional backhaul traffic, fail newly depleted nodes, refresh capabilities again, and record metrics. This ordering matters: a node recharged during harvesting can rejoin, while a missing lease may only be assigned at a later policy update.

Implementation evidence: simulation/runner.py: RoleSimulationModel.step

Panel prompt: Explain the implementation boundary and the tradeoff shown on this slide.
Node capability scoring
Gateway = 0.40E + 0.35Q + 0.25C
Anomaly detection = health monitoring = 0.50E + 0.50H
Discoverability = 0.34E + 0.33Q + 0.33H
Example: E=.9, H=.8, Q=.7, C=.6 gives gateway .755
Failed nodes contribute zero capability
nodes.py: ROLE_WEIGHTS; NodeAgent.capability

Define E as normalized battery energy, H as health, Q as node link quality, and C as normalized initial degree. ROLE_WEIGHTS in nodes.py is the single source of truth. Gateway capability in the example is .36 plus .245 plus .15, which is .755. Both anomaly detection and health monitoring produce .85 because their weight definitions are identical. Discoverability produces .801. Scores are bounded to [0,1]. A positive capability does not guarantee a route, which is why selection also checks reachability. No learned model or classifier appears here.

Implementation evidence: nodes.py: ROLE_WEIGHTS; NodeAgent.capability

Panel prompt: Explain the implementation boundary and the tradeoff shown on this slide.
Recursive capability aggregation
weighted_aggregate() uses normalized non-negative child weights
Missing child weights default to 1.0, so the default is a mean
Subnet vectors feed network vectors, then the internetwork vector
Failed children remain in the denominator with zero capability
Unequal child populations make a mean of means differ from a global node mean
simulation/capability.py: weighted_aggregate; refresh_capabilities

For child gateway scores .8 and .6 with weights 1 and 3, the aggregate is (.8 + 1.8) / 4 = .65. Empty children return a zero vector. Invalid negative weights or a nonpositive total raise an error. Refresh starts with all leaf vectors and updates each parent in dependency order. The default root gives equal weight to networks despite their 4/3/3 subnet counts. That is a hierarchy weighting choice, not a population-weighted global average. Recomputing from children keeps the function deterministic and independent of previous aggregate values.

Implementation evidence: simulation/capability.py: weighted_aggregate; refresh_capabilities

Panel prompt: Explain the implementation boundary and the tradeoff shown on this slide.
Selection and assignment
Candidates are immediate children of the requested scope
Filter unavailable entities and unreachable representatives
Choose maximum capability with a stable string-ID tie break
Send LEASE_GRANT before creating the active lease
Store leases in dict[(role, scope)] to enforce one holder per pair
simulation/protocols.py: _select_for_role; _assign

Explain _select_for_role and _assign together. A scope needs a control source and at least one reachable candidate. The proposed initial assignment is capability-based and does not deduct migration cost because no holder is being replaced. The hierarchical policy instead uses seeded random choice. A failed grant leaves the role unassigned. A successful grant creates a Lease and activates it. The tuple-keyed dictionary gives direct access to each role/scope assignment. Multiple roles may share a holder because the code has no capacity limit or exclusivity across different role keys.

Implementation evidence: simulation/protocols.py: _select_for_role; _assign

Panel prompt: Explain the implementation boundary and the tradeoff shown on this slide.
Lease lifecycle and epoch handling
pending
active
renewing
active
active
migrating
active
Expiry / invalidation ends a lease. Epoch retention can preserve holders.
simulation/leases.py; simulation/protocols.py: _advance_epoch; _lease_duration

The transitions library prohibits illegal jumps. New leases start pending and activate. Renewal temporarily enters renewing and updates timing before returning active. Migration enters migrating and replaces holder, epoch, and timing in the same lease object. Expiry or invalidation ends availability. Duration in proposed is 10 + capability times 90 by default, so a .8 score gives 82 ticks and renewal becomes due at 57.4 ticks, checked on integer ticks. Epochs advance every 20 ticks. Default behavior regrants assignments, while retention updates existing epoch labels in place. This is an in-process fencing model, not a distributed stale-message rejection protocol.

Implementation evidence: simulation/leases.py; simulation/protocols.py: _advance_epoch; _lease_duration

Panel prompt: Explain the implementation boundary and the tradeoff shown on this slide.
Cost-aware migration
Cost = α·2 + β·state_transfer + γ·route_cost·Econtrol + δ·disruption
Candidate utility = capability − λ·cost
Migrate only if best utility > current capability + Δ
Unreachable transfer routes have infinite cost and are excluded
simulation/protocols.py: calculate_migration_cost; _consider_cost_aware_migration

The cost terms are deterministic estimates. The control-message term is fixed at two, while _migrate sends one modeled MIGRATE exchange from the scope source to the new holder. Thus the utility estimate and actual charged control energy are related but distinct models. With route cost 6 and default control energy .00001, cost is .020 + .025 + .0006 + .050 = .0956. Candidate score .88 gives utility .87044. Against current .80 and delta .05, migration passes. A .85 candidate gives .84044 and fails. Optional cooldown and adaptive hysteresis can further restrict changes.

Implementation evidence: simulation/protocols.py: calculate_migration_cost; _consider_cost_aware_migration

Panel prompt: Explain the implementation boundary and the tradeoff shown on this slide.
Routing algorithm and example
Dijkstra minimizes sum of edge costs using a min-heap
Usable quality = base edge quality × min(endpoint link qualities)
Edge cost = 1 + 4 × (1 − quality)
Example: direct quality .2 costs 4.2, two quality .9 hops cost 2.8
Cache routes by source and invalidate after topology-affecting events
simulation/communications.py: _routes_from; _current_graph; find_route

This algorithm prefers the two-hop route in the example even though it uses more hops. A link at or below minimum_link_quality is excluded. Failed nodes lose incident usable links. Sorted neighbors and a numerical tolerance stabilize equal-cost behavior. Source equals destination returns a zero-hop successful route. A missing path returns None and increments a delivery-failure counter when a message is offered. Cache invalidation happens on failure, recovery, link degradation, and depletion. The router stores explicit path tuples for all reachable destinations, so path materialization adds overhead beyond the textbook Dijkstra bound.

Implementation evidence: simulation/communications.py: _routes_from; _current_graph; find_route

Panel prompt: Explain the implementation boundary and the tradeoff shown on this slide.
Communication and energy accounting
Count logical messages separately from message-hop transmissions
Each hop charges both transmitter and receiver
Transmit = Ebase × [1 + w × (distance / range)^p]
Receive = Ebase, with data and control using different base costs
Failed routing counts an offered item, while no route means no hop energy
simulation/communications.py: send; _hop_energy_cost; _record_energy; nodes.py

Default data energy is .00005 per endpoint and control energy .00001. Distance weight defaults to zero, while the stored clustered study uses weight one and exponent two. A zero-hop message succeeds without communication energy. Accounting records requested modeled costs even when battery depletion clamps the actual battery at zero, so communication energy and residual battery loss are not interchangeable conservation totals. Explicit degradation and harvested energy also change batteries. The model omits retransmissions, interference, sensing, CPU work, and idle consumption. All energy values use normalized units rather than joules.

Implementation evidence: simulation/communications.py: send; _hop_energy_cost; _record_energy; nodes.py

Panel prompt: Explain the implementation boundary and the tradeoff shown on this slide.
Solar harvesting and migration gate
Seeded node harvest = configured rate × uniform(.5, 1.5)
Battery capacity caps accepted harvest and records curtailed energy
Energy-depleted nodes rejoin after reaching the reserve threshold
Optional gate compares projected reserve benefit with transfer energy + margin
Failure replacement bypasses the optional migration gate
simulation/runner.py: _harvest_solar_energy; simulation/protocols.py: _solar_migration_is_worthwhile

Each node has a constant harvest rate for the entire run, with a separate seeded generator to avoid changing topology randomness. The projection uses battery plus horizon times harvest minus observed average communication use, then clamps capacity and subtracts essential reserve. Default horizon is 500 steps and margin is .01. Container reserve projections average available descendants. The gate does not replace capability and migration-cost ranking. It acts after hysteresis and applies only to optional migrations. This is a simple extrapolation without daylight or weather cycles, and the stored results must determine whether it actually helps.

Implementation evidence: simulation/runner.py: _harvest_solar_energy; simulation/protocols.py: _solar_migration_is_worthwhile

Panel prompt: Explain the implementation boundary and the tradeoff shown on this slide.
Data flow and persistence
Online sensor
Subnet gateway
Network gateway
Internetwork gateway
Sensor delivery measures the subnet leg.
Optional backhaul sends aggregates. Counters become CSV, PNG, and NPZ files.
simulation/runner.py: _route_sensor_traffic; simulation/metrics.py; simulation/experiments.py

Distinguish sensor-item delivery from hierarchical backhaul. Every currently online node offers one sensor item to its subnet gateway. The sensor delivery metric counts that first-leg success. When backhaul is enabled, successful subnets produce one aggregate to a network gateway, and active networks produce one aggregate to the internetwork gateway. Those aggregate deliveries have separate counters and do not redefine sensor-item delivery as end-to-end root receipt. Metrics accumulate in memory and export to CSV, PNG, and study NPZ files. There is no database, web API, or persistent server in this project.

Implementation evidence: simulation/runner.py: _route_sensor_traffic; simulation/metrics.py; simulation/experiments.py

Panel prompt: Explain the implementation boundary and the tradeoff shown on this slide.
Internal interfaces and failure handling
simulation/config.py; simulation/events.py; simulation/runner.py; simulation/communications.py

These are Python calls in one process, not HTTP endpoints. Configuration validates finite values, dimensions, ranges, and lease settings. Event construction rejects unsupported kinds and invalid degradation values. Model initialization rejects unknown node references and events beyond the configured horizon. Routing rejects invalid endpoint IDs but returns None for unavailable or disconnected endpoints. Lease transitions reject invalid lifecycle operations. Security is currently about input validation and state consistency. Authentication, authorization, encryption, and protection from malicious IoT nodes are absent because no actual network service is exposed.

Implementation evidence: simulation/config.py; simulation/events.py; simulation/runner.py; simulation/communications.py

Panel prompt: Explain the implementation boundary and the tradeoff shown on this slide.
Technical challenges and solutions
Roadmap.md; finished_work.md; simulation/metrics.py; simulation/protocols.py

These challenges are supported by code and development records rather than invented personal anecdotes. Early duplicated role weights motivated the single definition in nodes.py. Separating mesh from hierarchy prevents membership from silently creating radio links. The router separates logical messages from physical hop counts. The development record notes that 20-tick epoch revocation can mask longer lease renewal and batching behavior, leading to configurable retention. Explicit generated-item counts fix denominator ambiguity. A remaining concern is that shared memory gives immediate global capability knowledge unless periodic broadcasts are configured.

Implementation evidence: Roadmap.md; finished_work.md; simulation/metrics.py; simulation/protocols.py

test_nodes.py; tests/test_*.py

Panel prompt: Explain the implementation boundary and the tradeoff shown on this slide.
Stored experimental design
patent-study/run_patent_study.py; patent-study/results_20000/final_report.md

The supplied report declares 480 completed runs: 30 seeds times four scenarios times four arms. Seeds span 42–71 and each run lasts 20,000 ticks. Arms share the initial topology and event schedule within each seed and scenario. The study uses 100 nodes, intercluster gap 1.5 communication ranges, distance energy weight one, hierarchical backhaul, and epoch retention. Moderate harvest is .0002 before the seeded per-node multiplier. Because A and B also differ in controller and selection behavior, B minus A measures a bundled protocol contrast. C minus B isolates harvest within proposed, and D minus C isolates the optional gate.

Panel prompt: Explain the implementation boundary and the tradeoff shown on this slide.
Metric definitions and interpretation
CSC = available role-time intervals / required role-time intervals
Default denominator = 56 roles × elapsed ticks, excluding time zero
Sensor delivery = delivered sensor items / generated sensor items
Energy per item = modeled communication energy / delivered sensor items
Lifetime records first threshold crossing and right-censors absent crossings
simulation/metrics.py; patent-study/analyze_patent_study.py

CSC is a role-state availability proxy. It does not prove that anomaly detection or another application service performed useful computation. Sensor delivery includes unrouted generated items in the denominator, but only online nodes generate traffic, so compare offered load as well as fractions. It also measures the subnet leg rather than root delivery. The stored analyzer uses paired seed differences and 95 percent t intervals. Service lifetime uses cumulative fractions at 90 and 50 percent thresholds, while network lifetime uses instantaneous active-node fraction below 50 percent. Censored horizon values are not observed failure times.

Implementation evidence: simulation/metrics.py; patent-study/analyze_patent_study.py

Verified stored results: normal scenario
30 seeds per arm. Normalized energy units. Means of per-run ratios.
patent-study/results_20000/per_run_metrics.csv

preview: Arm | CSC | Sensor delivery | Energy/item ×10⁻⁶ | Total energy | Final battery

text:
These are per-run means recomputed from the supplied CSV, rounded for display. A retains substantial battery but loses much of the modeled service because coordination can fail. B has much higher role continuity and sensor delivery but low ending battery. C and D reach one in the stored sensor and continuity metrics under this configuration, with higher total communication energy because they sustain service longer. This is not evidence of perfect radio delivery in the field. Fractions are means of run fractions, and energy per item is the mean of per-run ratios, so it need not equal the ratio of displayed means.

What the paired comparisons support
Normal B − A sensor delivery: +68.02 percentage points
95% paired t interval: +65.68 to +70.35 percentage points
Normal C − B delivery: +16.62 percentage points
Normal D − C delivery: 0.00 percentage points
Normal D − C energy/item: +0.446 × 10⁻⁶ normalized units
patent-study/results_20000/paired_comparison.csv

Use percentage points for fraction differences. The stored normal B minus A delivery effect is .6801577 with interval [.6568311, .7034843]. C minus B is .1661842 with interval [.1554166, .1769518]. D minus C has zero delivery difference in normal, failures, and energy degradation. In link degradation its delivery interval includes zero. In normal, D slightly increases energy per delivered item, with a positive interval in the stored analysis. Therefore the gate does not establish a general improvement over harvest alone. These intervals describe this paired simulation design and do not establish causality for real devices or universal superiority.

Panel prompt: Explain the implementation boundary and the tradeoff shown on this slide.
Limitations
Role labels model availability, without anomaly detection or discovery payload algorithms
Shared-memory coordination does not simulate consensus, message delay, or split-brain
No MAC contention, retransmission, sensing / CPU energy, or calibrated radio units
Constant solar rates omit daylight and weather variation
Mesa version drift breaks startup, and SciPy is undeclared
simulation/entities.py; simulation/protocols.py; simulation/metrics.py; requirements.txt

Add several engineering subtleties if asked. Container representation is first available descendant, and initial degree centrality stays fixed. Role availability checks active lease, holder availability, and baseline controller availability, but does not test every application path. Broadcast snapshots default to immediate shared state because interval zero bypasses stale knowledge. Modeled energy counters can exceed actual removed battery energy near zero. The stored study has only one topology-size family and does not prove asymptotic scalability. Missing dependency pinning and an undeclared SciPy requirement reduce environment reproducibility. Fresh verification: Mesa 3.5.1 raises AttributeError when runner.py assigns scenario. Mesa 3.3.1 executes both smoke simulations. This is a concrete compatibility problem caused by the open mesa>=3 requirement, not just a hypothetical risk.

Implementation evidence: simulation/entities.py; simulation/protocols.py; simulation/metrics.py; requirements.txt

Panel prompt: Explain the implementation boundary and the tradeoff shown on this slide.
Future enhancements
Implement real role services with measurable task correctness
Add explicit message queues, delay, partition behavior, and stale-epoch rejection
Measure end-to-end root delivery with a fixed offered-load model
Calibrate radio and battery costs and introduce time-varying solar profiles
Pin dependencies and expand matched scaling and ablation experiments
Architectural recommendations based on simulation/ and study design

These are proposals, not existing features. A natural first extension is a service interface per role, separating assignment from service execution and defining useful work. Next introduce asynchronous messages and epoch validation at receivers, then test conflicting holders and network partitions. Track original sensor items through aggregates so root receipt can be measured. Add a realistic energy budget with idle, sensing, and CPU costs. For evaluation, isolate cost awareness, hysteresis, leases, and the gate rather than treating them as one bundle. Test more seeds, node counts, and parameter sensitivities before broad claims.

Close by returning to the research question: when is moving a role worth its communication cost? These are code-derived asymptotic interpretations, not measured benchmarks. Let N be physical nodes, E usable edges, K candidates for one role/scope, and R=4 roles. Topology compares node pairs. Aggregation sorts child IDs and performs weighted sums. Each uncached source builds Dijkstra routes, then materializes each destination path. In a chain the sum of path lengths is quadratic. Its capability becomes zero but its child weight remains in the denominator, reducing the parent aggregate.

When are cached routes invalidated?
Failure, recovery, link degradation, and depletion invalidate usable graph and source-route caches.
What is the routing complexity caveat?
Heap-based shortest paths are followed by explicit reconstruction of every destination path. Path storage can dominate textbook distance-only bounds.
How is solar energy modeled?
A constant seeded per-node rate charges batteries up to capacity. Overflow is curtailed, and depleted nodes rejoin after reaching reserve.
Can the solar gate block failure recovery?
No. The gate restricts optional migrations. Assignment after holder failure takes the recovery path instead.
